summary: Describes the individuals and organizations involved in the IETF standards process (BCP 9), with short descriptions of each entity and its role. It reflects the IETF's changed structure and obsoletes RFC 2028 from 1996. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: Making Internet standards takes many people and groups. This is the who's who, saying what each one does so newcomers know who is who.

questions: who is involved in the ietf standards process
what are the roles of iesg and iab
subtitle: A who's who of the people and organizations behind the IETF standards process.

tldr.problem: The IETF's structure changed a great deal after RFC 2028 was published in 1996, so its description of who does what in the standards process was out of date.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9281 briefly describes the key individual roles (document editor, working group chair, area director) and key organizations (IETF, working groups, IESG, IAB, RPC, IANA, IRTF, IETF Trust, IETF LLC, Secretariat, ISOC) and what each does.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 11) that obsoletes RFC 2028 and complements BCP 9, which defines the standardization process itself.

today: RFC 9281 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2022. It obsoletes RFC 2028 and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Purpose and Changes Since RFC 2028
sections.content:
The process the IETF community uses to standardize protocols and procedures is described in BCP 9. BCP 9 defines the stages, the requirements for moving a document between stages and the types of documents used. RFC 9281 identifies some of the key individual roles and organizations in that process.

The document refers to roles in the singular, such as "a document editor", although many roles are filled by more than one person. It obsoletes RFC 2028. The changes, in no particular order, include adding the responsible area director role and reordering the roles to follow the typical workflow, adding the IETF Administration LLC and the IETF Trust, renaming "RFC Editor" to "RFC Production Center" to reflect RFC 9280, and adding Terminology and Acknowledgements sections.
sections.eli5: An old who's who list from 1996 no longer matched how the group works, so this is the updated version.

sections.title: Key Individuals
sections.content:
The roles are listed roughly in the order in which they get involved. A document editor is designated by the working group chair and ensures that a document accurately reflects the decisions the working group has made. If the editor is also a chair of the same group, another chair should manage the process for that document. If none is available, the group and the area director must watch the process especially carefully.

A working group chair facilitates the group's activities, presides over its meetings and makes sure its commitments are met. The chair is the formal point of contact between the group and the IESG, via the group's area director.

Each working group is assigned a single responsible area director (AD). The AD can help the chair assess consensus, reviews documents after the group approves them, and coordinates the IESG review and IETF Last Call. An AD can also sponsor an Internet-Draft directly, though this is not very common, and no working group is involved then. Except for the General Area, IETF areas traditionally have multiple ADs.
sections.eli5: The editor writes down what the team decided, the chair runs the team's meetings, and the area director is the grown-up who checks the work before it goes further.

sections.title: The IETF and Its Working Groups
sections.content:
The IETF is an open international community of network designers, operators, implementors, researchers and other interested parties, and is the principal body developing new Internet Standard specifications. Its technical work is done in working groups (WGs), organized by topic into areas, each under the coordination of an AD. WGs have a narrow focus and a lifetime bounded by their charter and milestones, though some are long-lived. "Dispatch" WGs assess where new work should be done and do not directly produce standards.

Membership is established solely by individuals who participate. They do not formally represent organizations they are affiliated with. Anyone with the time and interest may take part and attend IETF meetings, which are usually held three times a year, and active participation is possible without attending in person. Participants must disclose relevant intellectual property rights that are reasonably and personally known to them when they take part in discussions about a specific technology. New WGs are established by the IESG and almost always have an explicit charter.
sections.eli5: The IETF is an open club where anyone interested can join a small team that works on one topic. Each team has a clear job and stops when it is done.

sections.title: The Steering and Oversight Bodies
sections.content:
The IESG manages the IETF's technical activities and administers the standards process under the rules in BCP 9. It handles initial approval of new WGs, rechartering and final approval of documents. It is composed of the ADs and the IETF Chair, who also chairs the IESG and is the AD for the General Area. The IAB Chair is an ex officio member.

The IAB provides oversight of the architecture of the Internet and its protocols, and of the standards process. It approves the IESG candidates put forward by the Nominations Committee (NomCom), reviews all proposed WG charters, and serves as an appeal board for complaints about improper execution of the process. IAB members are nominated by the NomCom and confirmed by the ISOC Board. The IETF Chair is a member of the IAB and the IRTF Chair is ex officio.

The IRTF focuses on longer-term research as a parallel organization to the IETF. Its research groups publish results that can also appear as RFCs on the IRTF Stream, but their contributions carry no more weight in the IETF than other community input.
sections.eli5: One group of grown-ups runs the day-to-day work, another watches the big picture and settles complaints, and a research club explores ideas for later.

sections.title: Publication, Registries and Administration
sections.content:
The RFC Production Center (RPC) handles editorial preparation and publication of RFCs. RFC policy is defined by the RFC Series Working Group and approved by the RFC Series Advisory Board. The details are in RFC 9280.

IANA assigns values for protocol parameters that must be uniquely assigned, such as port numbers and option identifiers, and maintains the registries. Assignments are coordinated through an "IANA Considerations" section in each document. IANA also operates parts of the DNS and coordinates IP address assignments.

The IETF Trust is the legal owner of intellectual property for the IETF, IRTF and IAB, including trademarks and the copyrights to RFCs. The IETF Administration LLC provides the corporate legal home for the IETF, IAB and IRTF, supports operations, manages finances and budget, and signs contracts for the Secretariat, meeting hotels and tools contractors. The IETF Secretariat, contracted by the IETF LLC, handles meeting logistics and maintains the formal public record of the standards process. The Internet Society (ISOC) hosts the IETF LLC, appoints the NomCom Chair, confirms IAB candidates and acts as the final authority in the appeals process.
sections.eli5: Other groups print the finished documents, hand out the unique numbers, keep the legal papers, pay the bills and keep the meeting records.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no new security considerations, and that it has no IANA actions. It is a descriptive document about people and organizations, not a protocol, so there are no message formats or registries to specify.
sections.eli5: This is just a list of who does what, so there is nothing new to protect or register.
